text.p: By hauling a string of caravans up a West Bank hill under cover of darkness, Jewish settlers have shone a light on the apparent land-or-peace dilemma facing Benjamin Netanyahu, the man they helped elect as Israel's prime minister.
Netanyahu is under U.S. and international pressure to honour peace deals with the Palestinians which entail withdrawing from areas of the West Bank that settlers deem Jewish by God-given right.
But the Likud party leader also has to hold together a centre-right coalition government whose influential right-wing is made up of settlers, idealogues and diehard Zionists.
They oppose any withdrawal including an Israeli redeployment in Hebron which should have taken place under the Labour government Netanyahu toppled last May.
Up to seven cabinet ministers have indicated they would vote against the Hebron redeployment deal which U.S. envoy Dennis Ross is trying to broker.

Such a cabinet revolt is unlikely to bring down the government, political analysts say. But it could make Netanyahu even more reluctant to implement the withdrawals from West Bank villages called for after Hebron in the 1993 Oslo agreement on Palestinian self-rule.
This is certainly the fear of Palestinians, who reacted angrily to the settlers' placing of mobile homes on a hilltop last Friday near the settlement of Beit El, north of Jerusalem.

"This is another attempt by the settlers to undermine the chances of reaching a deal on Hebron and on redeployment in 'C' areas," said Palestinian analyst and former negotiator Ziad Abu Zayyad. Area C is the West Bank land peppered with some 140 Jewish settlements and Israeli military installations.
"Settlers provocations are likely to increase as the chances of a Hebron agreement draw closer," Abu Zayyad told Reuters.

Settler leaders say their protests are not connected to Hebron. They say they do not want to embarrass Netanyahu. But their actions give the Israeli leader problems with his Palestinian peace partners and main ally Washington.
"This is a protest action," said Aharon Domb, a spokesman for the settler umbrella group YESHA.

"There is a bitter spirit between YESHA and the prime minister," he told Reuters. He said Beit El settlers were angry at the government's delay in allowing them to expand their settlement as a response to the killing by Palestinian gunmen of a settler and her son last month.

"My estimate is that if they do not receive permits they will go up the hill again," Domb added. The settlers came down from the hill but left their caravans there pending a deal with the government. In many similar stand-offs since Israel captured the West Bank in 1967 the settlers have eventually won out.
"They are trying to measure the strength of Netanyahu and find out how much he is committed to expand settlements," said Meiron Benvenisti, an Israeli expert on settlement.

"This is just a trial balloon. I don't think basically they are trying to embarrass Netanyahu but it's a way to test his will to continue and no doubt undermine the imminent signing of the Hebron deal," Benvenisti told Reuters.

Since taking office in July Netanyahu has authorised the building of some 3,000 homes in existing settlements, according to Israeli peace activist figures. But he has not started new settlements, an action that would cross a red line even for President Bill Clinton, who has voiced some of the warmest support for Israel of any U.S. administration, diplomats say.
Washington was irked last month by Netanyahu's reinstatement of benefits and tax breaks to the 130,000 settlers in the West Bank and Gaza.

Palestinians fear these incentives will draw more Israelis to their land which is being criss-crossed under a government building programme by new roads and tunnels to speed Jews from settlements to jobs in West Jerusalem and Tel Aviv.
Palestinian legislator Hanan Ashrawi called the Beit El action not only a provocation to Arabs but to Netanyahu.

"If they are allowed to continue to present this challenge, this direct threat to the policy making in Israel and to the peace process itself, then I think they are capable of destroying the chances of peace and plunging us back again in to an unholy cycle of violence. They have to be stopped," she told Reuters.
Palestinian leaders acknowledge Netanyahu has coalition problems but they insist he honour Israel's internationally-sponsored peace commitments.
"The Israeli government should not use the excuse of opposition to escape its obligations," said Abu Zayyad.
Analysts said all parties would be watching to see whether, in the words of one Western envoy, Netanyahu allowed himself to become hostage to the settlers.

"The settlers want to find out how he is going to react," Benvenisti said. "This is part of the campaign in the government, in the cabinet and also now in extra-parliamentary cirlces, to intimidate Netanyahu."
"I don't think Netanyahu will give in. I dont think the settlers expect this," he added.
